item.title: What if the Falcons win/lose against the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2026
item.description: A new season is upon us
item.content:encoded:
We’re at the starting line of yet another NFL season, as the Atlanta Falcons look to fight their way out of the wilderness. The team made headlines this offseason by cleaning house from top to bottom and replacing all of the primary decision makers in Flowery Branch, booting away Raheem Morris, Terry Fontenot and Rich McKay after another period of failure.

Now, with Matt Ryan, Ian Cunningham and Kevin Stefanski at the helm, Atlanta looks to transition into a period of prosperity, something they haven’t had since Ryan himself was operating under center as the team’s quarterback.

We will go game by game with the Falcons throughout the season answering two simple questions before each game — what will happen from a scenario perspective if they win this coming week, as well as if they lose.

The Falcons are currently in the midst of a nine year playoff draught, the second-longest active streak in the NFL. If they win and are in contention for a post season spot, this series will be looking at possible playoff and division based scenarios. Conversely, if they go the familiar route of losing too much, this will become a series looking at draft based scenarios.

Let’s get right into it then for the 2026 season. Here is the scenario the Falcons face if they beat the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 1, as well as if they lose.

If the Falcons win

It will be a dream start for Kevin Stefanski, who will become the first non-interim Falcons head coach to start his tenure with a victory since Dan Quinn’s victory on Monday Night Football in 2015. He will do so by beating a team he faced as a division rival the last six seasons, in Cleveland, as well.

The Falcons themselves will get off to their first 1-0 start since beating Carolina at home in 2023, and will avenge a 2024 home defeat against the Steelers in that season opener, which was also Raheem Morris’ first game in his new Falcons tenure. This would also be just the second time Atlanta won game one of the season since 2017, which is also the last time they made it to the playoffs.

This would not be a victory against just any opponent — it would be just Atlanta’s third triumph over the Steelers in 20 tries, historically. Pittsburgh is the team that has beaten the Falcons more thoroughly than anybody else according to win percentage. This would be the Birds’ first win in this matchup in exactly two decades; it would also be their first victory in Pittsburgh ever.

The Falcons have a home game against a Panthers team that’s had their number in recent memory coming up, and going into that game with a 1-0 record will not only increase their confidence but it would relieve any pressure of potentially digging themselves into an 0-2 hole from the jump.

If the Falcons lose

It will be more of the same historically — another head coach starting his Falcons career off with a defeat, another season starting 0-1, another loss to the Steelers specifically. Following a turbulent training camp and preseason period, the fanbase will likely be a bit more distraught than usual with another poor start.

Stefanski’s own personal record against the Steel Curtain will fall to 6-8 (6-7 with Cleveland which, all things considered is pretty good given how bad the Browns have historically been in that matchup since becoming reestablished as a franchise).

Atlanta’s schedule this season isn’t what I would consider light. Early on, their upcoming games in the immediate aftermath of this one will be against a Panthers team that swept them last season followed by a Thursday night trip to Lambeau Field to face a very good Packers team. This isn’t even getting to the difficult part of the schedule yet. Things could begin getting a bit dire quickly if they start out with a defeat right from the jump.

item.title: Giants to unveil new-look, physical offense against Cowboys
item.description: Can the Giants put up points on Dallas’ reworked defense?
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants are looking to start the John Harbaugh era off with a bang, and come away from their season-opening Sunday Night Football game with a win over the Dallas Cowboys.

The matchup between the Giants’ offense and Cowboys’ defense is one of the most intriguing of the weekend. The Giants’ offense will look significantly different from a year ago, with Jaxson Dart at quarterback, Darnell Mooney, Odell Beckham Jr., and Malachi Fields at receiver, Isaiah Likely at tight end, Patrick Ricard at fullback, and a new coaching staff.

The Cowboys, meanwhile have a reshuffled roster of their own and a completely new scheme under Christian Parker.

As things stand now, we simply don’t quite know what either unit will look like or how they’ll play.

So what can we expect when Jaxson Dart and the Giants’ offense takes the field against the Cowboys’ defense? Let’s start with what we do know and then make some educated guesses.

What will the Giants’ offense look like?

This has been, perhaps, the most beguiling question hanging over the Giants’ offseason — at least for me. The Giants having four former offensive coordinators on their staff (OC Matt Nagy, QB coach/passing game coordinator Brian Callahan, senior assistant Greg Roman, and tight ends coach Tim Kelly) may not be unprecedented, but it is unorthodox.

We won’t really know how it will work until the game is well under way. However my personal speculation has been that Nagy will serve as the master distiller who blends various aspects of Roman, Callahan, and Kelly’s philosophies into a single product. It could blow up in the Giants’ faces, or the various twists on existing schemes could present defenses with unexpected looks or combinations of concepts.

That said, we might be able to use context clues to define the negative space and get a rough outline of what the Giants want to do on offense.

Power running game – This one became blatantly obvious when the Giants hired John Harbaugh and painfully obvious when they hired Greg Roman as “Senior Offensive Assistant”. Harbaugh has always favored a run-heavy offense, while Roman loves a down-hill rushing attack and is among the best in the NFL at scheming one up. The Giants will likely attempt to displace the defense vertically and force them to crowd the box. We’ll also likely see Jaxson Dart used as a runner more than those fearing the Blue Tent would likely prefer. After all, John Harbaugh was once called the “Prince Of Analytics” by ESPN, and forcing defenses to play true 11-on-11 football is typically confers an analytic advantage for the offense.

Heavy sets – Again, this one is pretty obvious based on John Harbaugh’s past preferences. It was only reinfoced when the Giants released Darius Slayton and left themselves with just four receivers. That doesn’t mean the Giants will forego the passing attack, but rather they’ll be getting their tight ends and backs heavily involved as pass catchers. Isaiah Likely was Jaxson Dart’s most common target in training camp, while Theo Johnson flashed brilliance (in addition to frustrating drops) in his second season. Likewise, each of the Giants’ four running backs are dangerous pass catchers. Former receiver Tyrone Tracy is the obvious standout, however Cam Skattebo, Najee Harris, and Devin Singletary all have upside as pass catchers.

Precision passing game – Teams often like contrast between their running and passing game. So if the Giants want a downhill rushing attack, we could see that paired with a passing attack that uses precise route running to set receivers up for yards after the catch. This is where Brian Callahan’s influence (may) come in. Where Matt Nagy is a traditional West Coast Offense guy, having learned under Andy Reid, Callahan comes from the “New West Coast” tree. In other words, we could see influences from the “Kubiak-Shanahan-McVay” school of offense. In that vein, it’s notable that the Giants’ four remaining receivers are all talented route runners. Even 6-foot-4, 220-pound rookie Malachi Fields is far more nimble than his frame would suggest.

The release of Slayton may also suggest that Malik Nabers is trending toward being ready to play Week 1.

There will certainly be a vertical aspect to the offense, Lamar Jackson was tied for the fourth-highest intended air yardage in the NFL last year (9.1 yards downfield), while Matt Stafford was third with 9.2 intended air yards. So while much of the passing attack may be to set Malik Nabers and Darnell Mooney up with YAC opportunities, we should also expect to see the Giants attempt to generate chunk plays.

Condensed sets – Modern NFL offenses like to weaponize every aspect of play design, including formation width. While spread formations can be conducive to running the ball (by forcing defenses to spread out an lighten the box), condensed sets are coming into vogue. The Giants featuring tight ends and a fullback suggests that they’ll go with that trend, though perhaps not for the reason fans expect. Condensed sets certainly make it easier to insert receivers or detached tight ends into gaps as blockers for inside runs. But they also allow offenses to create traffic for their passing concepts. That, in turn, makes play-action passes to the intermediate area even more effective and can force teams to pay for playing a base defense.

The Fangio factor

In addition to not knowing quite what to expect from the Giants’ offensive scheme to start the season, we also don’t know quite what to expect from the Dallas defense either.

The Cowboys fired their previous defensive coordinator after fielding a historically bad defense for much of the 2025 season, and hired former Philadelphia Eagles Passing Game Coordinator and defensive backs coach Christian Parker. Parker spent 2024 and 2025 with the Cowboys after spending 2022 and 2023 as the Denver Broncos’ defensive backs coach.

Parker is considered one of the bright young minds on the defensive side of the ball and is a disciple of Eagles’ DC Vic Fangio. In other words, we should expect the new-look Cowboys’ defense to be similar in structure to what the Eagles run.

The Fangio scheme is based on quarters coverages, man-match coverage rules, nickel sets, and post-snap rotations.

Coverage rotations are a signature aspect of Fangio’s scheme, usually starting out in quarters coverages and rotating to a Cover 3 look, or to Cover 6 and Cover 8 looks. Cover 6 and Cover 8 are hybrid coverages that mix Cover 2 and Cover 4 principles. The primary difference is that Cover 6 plays the “quarters” side to the passing strength, while Cover 8 plays the “quarters” away from the passing strength.

The purpose of the rotations is to disguise rotations, help simulate pressure, and allow nickel sets to play heavier than they appear on paper.

Speaking of nickel sets, while the “Fangio” defense is based in the 3-4, his primary alignments are 4-2-5 Nickel and 3-3-5 Penny sets. In either case, STAR Caleb Downs will be a key piece for the Dallas defense as the third DB. He’ll be playing a similar role as Cooper DeJean does in Philly, and be Dallas’ primary “Pivot” player who changes the look between Quarters, Cover 6, and Cover 8, as well as changing how Dallas defends gaps up front.

The Giants will likely want to go back and study last year’s Week 8 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles in preparation for this game. The Giants trounced the Eagles just two weeks prior, however that game featured Fangio abandoning his usual tendencies to attack the rookie QB with blitzes. Jaxson Dart comported himself well in that game, but struggled once Fangio returned to his usual defense in Week 8. Dart will need to prove that he can decipher the

Ultimately, there are two big questions with respect to the Cowboys’ defense: First, whether they have the personnel to properly run a Fangio-adjacent defense. It’s one of the most popular schemes in the NFL for a reason, but is not easy to implement. Second, can Parker recognize the weaknesses in the defense well enough to account for them? Perhaps Fangio’s greatest strength is that he understands how to attack his own defense and anticipates how opposing offenses will do so. Does Parker have enough experience to do the same?

Matchups to watch

The Giants iOL vs. the Cowboys iDL

This might be the matchup that determines the course of the game. If I had to point to the strength of the Dallas’ personnel, it would be DTs Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark. Both Williams and Clark outclass any of the Giants’ interior linemen.

As a practical matter, the Giants’ success in the middle will likely to whether they’re able to manipulate the math up front. The Giants’ blockers don’t need to dominate the match-up if they can account for Williams and Clark with their scheme without weakening their blocking elsewhere.

Patrick Ricard, Isaiah Likely, and Theo Johnson vs. the Dallas linebackers (and Caleb Downs)

This is, of course, downstream of the previous matchup.

While Dallas’ defensive tackles are formidable, their second level players are all on the light side. LB DeMarvion Overshown is listed at 6-foot-3, 230 pounds, LB Dee Winters is listed at 5-foot-11, 227 pounds, and STAR Caleb Downs is listed at 6-foot, 206 pounds.

Both Overshown and Winters are athletic (though neither is quite as athletic as Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese), while Downs is a fast processor. The question in the run game is whether they can insert themselves into gaps before the Giants’ secondary blockers (Ricard, Likely, and Johnson) can get there. The Giants will almost certainly use their big skill position players as lead or insert blockers to account for Dallas’ second level players trying to gap out the Giants’ offense.

In the passing game, is their athleticism enough to compensate for Likely and Johnson’s size advantage? As mentioned up top, the Giants will likely be relying on their tight ends and backs as pass catchers out of heavy personnel in condensed sets. Can the Giants use their size to their advantage in the middle of the field?

Malik Hooker, Jalen Thompson, and Caleb Downs vs. Jaxson Dart

No, the Giants’ offensive coordinator won’t be on the field. However, as we talked about earlier, Christian Parker is expected to employ a “Fangio Adjacent” scheme, which will likely live in a 3-safety nickel set. They want to use their safeties as adjustment players to rotate between coverage looks, disguise (or simulate) pressure, and muddy the offensive reads.

It’ll be up to Jaxson Dart to quickly and accurately diagnose the Cowboys’ defense. The Fangio defense is based out of quarters coverage, but likes to employ rotations to Cover 3, as well as Cover 6 and Cover 8. Each of those coverages has weaknesses that can be exploited, but the next step for Dart will be deciphering them and making the correct decision. While Clark and Willimas are the Cowboys’ best defenders, cracking their safeties will likely be the key to the defense.

item.title: Panthers vs Bears: Matchups to watch
item.description: We look at two key match-ups on the field and one bonus match-up that could decide the outcome of Panthers vs Bears.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL season is off and running. We got our first ever Wednesday night opener and we’re going to get our first ever game in Australia of all places on Thursday. The league will get back to normal on Sunday, and the Carolina Panthers will play host to the Chicago Bears when that happens.

These two teams share a link with one another that’s going to give meetings between them a little extra juice. The teams essentially swapped first overall picks in 2023 and 2024, resulting in Bryce Young landing in Carolina and Caleb Williams landing in Chicago. Both teams ascended to the playoffs last season but did so with lots of late winners and close game luck. Both are looking to prove that last season wasn’t a fluke and that they are going to be players when the postseason comes around in a few months.

There are a fair few similarities in the roster constructions as well, and that makes for some interesting match-ups across both units. We’re going to look at one of those match-ups on each side of the ball.

The Panthers defensive front vs the Bears offensive line

The Bears had one of the best offensive lines in the NFL last season. According to ESPN’s pass block win rate statistic, the Bears were the best team in the league at protecting their quarterback, and they’re returning most of the key components from that unit. Darnell Wright, who the Bears picked with the first round pick they received in the Bryce Young draft, is one of the best right tackles in the league. Jonah Jackson and Joe Thuney are an elite guard duo, while Braxton Jones will retake his starting left tackle spot that he vacated due to injury last year. The one exception is at center. Last year, Drew Dalman earned a Pro Bowl spot for his elite play at that spot, but he surprisingly retired this past offseason at age 27. They’re replacing him with Garrett Bradbury, a Charlotte native who has just been a serviceable center to this point in his career.

On the other side of the line is a Panthers front that has struggled to generate pressure for several seasons now. They ranked 24th in pass rush win rate last season, so they went out and spent big money on Jaelan Phillips to try to rectify that. He’ll have his hands full trying to make an impact against such a formidable tackle duo, so the real difference maker here might have to be Derrick Brown. He had a career high five sacks last season, and he’s the best interior presence the Panthers have. He’ll probably spend most of his time against the guards, but he should get some pass rush opportunities over Bradbury, who projects to be the weak point on this offensive line. He and rookie Lee Hunter on early downs will need to make some noise to mitigate the advantage the Bears offense has in the trenches.

Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker vs the Bears secondary

The Bears overcame a brutal defense to make the playoffs last season, so they devoted their offseason to revamping that group. The biggest overhaul came in the secondary, but their big signing, cornerback Coby Bryant, is already out for the season with a knee injury. That leaves the Bears relying on Tyrique Stevenson (of Commanders Hail Mary fame) as their number two corner, which is exactly what they were trying to avoid by signing Bryant. Starting nickel Kyler Gordon is also out, leaving the Bears to rely on Cam Lewis to start in that spot. Their new starting safety duo is rookie Dillon Thieneman and veteran Xavier Woods, who Panthers fans should be familiar with.

Jaylon Johnson is very good, so he’ll give problems to whoever is lined up across from him. Any other receiver on the field should be expected to have success. The unit has a reputation for catastrophic breakdowns in coverage, which should open up big play opportunities for McMillan and Coker. They need to capitalize on those opportunities and find the space provided to them, and quarterback Bryce Young needs to find those breakdowns in coverage and make some throws down the field.

Bryce Young vs Week 1

This will be Young’s fourth Week 1. In his first three, he completed 49.5% of his passes for 4.4 yards per attempt (153.7 yards per game) with two touchdowns and six interceptions. It’s been nothing but bad. He’s entering a make or break year as it pertains to his future in Carolina. He can’t afford to start off so poorly once again.

item.title: The Packers’ defense was the opposite of the Seahawks last season
item.description: Seattle essentially allows Nick Emmanwori to play linebacker. Green Bay hasn’t done the same with Javon Bullard
item.content:encoded:
Here’s an interesting stat that I saw last night during the NFL regular-season opener, when the Seattle Seahawks were able to take down the New England Patriots in the Super Bowl rematch. According to Sümer Sports, the 2025 Seahawks played five defensive backs 81 percent of the time when opposing offenses played two or fewer receivers, which led the NFL, while the Green Bay Packers did so on just 14 percent of snaps, the second-lowest rate in the league, only behind the Detroit Lions.

That might be a little wordy, so I want to break this down piece by piece.

Generally, NFL defenses tend to match the number of outside cornerbacks and slot defenders on the field to the number of receivers the opposing offense throws out there. Why? So they can have bigger bodies on the grass against heavier personnel sets (like multi-tight end or multi-back looks) when teams are running the ball more frequently, and so they don’t have to play a linebacker in coverage against a slot receiver in three-receiver sets, when opposing offenses pass the ball more.

Under defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley, the Packers stuck to their “matching” personnel rules pretty strictly, outside of the red zone and short-yardage plays. To me, it’s not a surprise that they only broke “matching” personnel 14 percent of the time. In fact, I was a little surprised it was that high. If you only measured plays between the 20s, that number probably drops.

Meanwhile, the Seahawks, who play a quarters-based scheme that new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon is expected to run in Green Bay, played their nickel or dime subpackages on more than four-fifths of their plays when they got heavy personnel looks from the offensive side of the ball. For perspective, only five teams in the entire NFL didn’t match heavy personnel with primarily a “base” defense last year, and two of those — the San Francisco 49ers and Buffalo Bills — barely crossed the threshold with a 51 percent rate.

The reason that Seattle can do this is that Nick Emmanwori, the Seahawks’ slot defender, essentially can play both as a slot defender and as a Sam linebacker. For the most part, a slot defender in a 4-2 nickel look is basically playing the 4-3 Sam linebacker role anyway, just split out from the formation when the slot receiver is detached from the formation. When that slot receiver motions into the formation, potentially as an insert player to help run block, the slot defender usually travels with him, putting the slot defender in a more traditional Sam linebacker role pre-snap.

The Seahawks seem perfectly fine allowing Emmanwori to play both of those spots, no matter what opposing offenses throw out on the field. Meanwhile, the Packers haven’t been as confident in their slot defender, Javon Bullard, right or wrong.

Gannon’s Cardinals didn’t match heavy personnel on 23 percent of snaps last year, a good jump up from the Packers’ 14 percent mark in 2025, but still nowhere near the Seahawks’ 81 percent rate.

In the NFL of old, a slot defender and a slot receiver were both of the mold of players who were too small to play on the outside. Now, with how run games want to manipulate both positions, those players are much bigger, as slot defenders are also asked to be Sam linebackers and slot receivers are being asked to play some tight end-like roles. It should be no surprise that defenses with Emmanwori (6’2”, 220 pounds) and Kyle Hamilton (6’4”, 218 pounds) are the most comfortable in just letting their nickel personnel stay on the field and having their slot defenders add on as a strong-side linebacker.

For what it’s worth, and it’s only the preseason, Gannon’s defense in the preseason typically matched personnel with the opposing offense. Maybe we’ll see his unit play more six-defensive-back looks against multi-tight-end sets in the regular season, though, as the team has shown a three-safety Penny defense, built to stop the run with extra defensive backs on the field, during the summer.

Cam Ward’s preseason struggles can’t go unnoticed, and the Jets had a solid offseason, bringing in veteran defensive talent like Minkah Fitzpatrick and Demario Davis while drafting pass rusher David Bailey.

With fellow draft picks Kenyon Sadiq Jr. and Omar Cooper Jr. set to carve out nice roles in the offense alongside Geno Smith and Garrett Wilson, give me the Jets to start 2026 on a high note.

As a Colts fan, I’m going to savor the brief window of seeing Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward on the field together before the injury gods inevitably send one (or both) to IR.

The Ravens should be excellent under Jesse Minter in the long run, but losing All-Pro center Tyler Linderbaum could create some early hiccups for their offense.

Give me Indy to pull off the home upset at Lucas Oil Stadium. For the Shoe!

Falcons vs. Steelers: Steelers (63%)

Atlanta went full “28-3 mode” this offseason, losing both Jalon Walker and James Pearce Jr. to injury and suspension.

Add in a messy QB battle between Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr., and the Falcons dominated my Twitter FYP for all the wrong reasons.

More continuity around Aaron Rodgers and the Steelers in Year 2 will give them a leg up at home.

The Panthers came back down to earth in the second half of last season, going just 3-5 SU over their final eight games. Now, they enter Week 1 with an already banged-up offensive line.

Ben Johnson will be looking for Caleb Williams and the Bears to make an early statement in the NFC, and Chicago will do just that in Charlotte.

Deshaun Watson as the starter? Really?

Washington’s offensive line is an unmitigated disaster, and at this point, the Eagles losing A.J. Brown feels more like an addition than a subtraction for the psyche of Jalen Hurts and the Philly offense.

Eric Bieniemy will likely take a conservative approach, leaning heavily on Kenneth Walker III and the Chiefs’ ground game as Patrick Mahomes works his way back into form.

item.title: 5 Qs Lions vs. Saints preview: How New Orleans will navigate early-season injuries
item.description: Here’s our preview with Canal Street Chronicles about this Week 1 matchup between the Detroit Lions and New Orleans Saints.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL season is officially underway after Wednesday’s game between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks got things kicked off. Thursday, you can throw another shrimp on the barbie because there’s more opening week football coming your way. But if you’re reading this, it’s easy to assume you’re most excited for a game taking place at 1 p.m. ET at Ford Field.

Welcome back, football. We’ve been waiting for you.

This week, we had the pleasure of connecting with Nic Jennings, a writer for Canal Street Chronicles, to give us some insight into who these New Orleans Saints are heading into 2026. We learned what Tyler Shough needs to do to take the next step in his development, which skill position players are going to step up in the case of injuries, and what the defensive line is capable of doing—and much more.

1. The Saints are entering Year 2 under Kellen Moore—once a fixture of sports talk radio in Detroit when he was backing up Matthew Stafford. New Orleans looked like they were making some strides late last season, so what are the expectations for Moore in his second season, and where did you hear/see about that momentum from last year carrying over into this summer/preseason for the Saints?

The expectations are definitely higher for Kellen Moore this time around.

The locker room clearly responds to him and never lost morale when things were rocky to start last season, but with winning expectations replacing a rebuilding mindset in 2026, Moore is going to have to keep that fire and intensity to set the tone for the group. The cultural improvement and overall vibe around this team have been undeniable since his arrival in New Orleans, but now they need to turn that into wins.

More importantly, rather than coming straight off a Super Bowl victory, Moore had his first full offseason to build this team his way this time around. I think the personnel changes could be significant. He brought in guys who fit what he wants to do offensively while also adding another strong draft class. And honestly, the NFC South is there for the taking. It’s a relatively weak division, so if New Orleans can get off to a strong start and Moore can keep his team prepared to compete, I think they have a legitimate opportunity to surprise some people.

2. New Orleans will be without a couple of skill position players in Week 1 against Detroit, including Alvin Kamara and first-round pick Jordyn Tyson. What do you think the depth chart looks like at those positions heading into this matchup, and how do you think those players will be utilized?

In terms of the Saints’ pass catchers, expect to see a hefty dose of All-Pro Chris Olave. The duo of Olave and Tyler Shough could truly end up being one of the league’s better pairings based on what we saw from them down the final stretch of last season and throughout this year’s training camp, including three joint practices. Their chemistry only seems to be getting stronger.

Devaughn Vele, who has emerged as one of Shough’s go-to targets over the middle and in contested situations, also finished last season strong, while Juwan Johnson is coming off a career year and can extend drives with his YAC abilities. Then you have rookies Barion Brown and Bryce Lance, who have continued to impress and have given the coaching staff no reason to believe they can’t make an impact this season. The Saints triple-dipped at receiver in the draft, and while Jordyn Tyson is currently out, Brown and Lance both look like potential studs. Brown in particular really looks like a star in the making. At tight end behind Johnson, rookie Oscar Delp and veteran Noah Fant could also find themselves involved.

For the ball carriers, New Orleans obviously added Travis Etienne Jr. this offseason, and I expect to see a ton of him in Detroit. He fits what Kellen Moore wants to do offensively, whether it’s his speed and explosive-play ability or his value as a pass catcher. Kendre Miller also looks to finally be healthy and has always impressed when he’s been on the field. This team is better with him, but he simply hasn’t been able to stay healthy, so I expect him to have a chip on his shoulder and try to make a statement.

With Devin Neal no longer in the picture, keep an eye on Audric Estime as well. He’s taken advantage of every opportunity he’s been given and really finished last season on a strong note. He could be another player who earns a bigger role than expected.

3. Losing Bryan Bresee to a torn ACL on the first day of training camp is a tough blow for the interior of that defensive line. Who are some of the players New Orleans will turn to in his absence, and what is your level of confidence in that group coming into Week 1?

It is definitely a tough blow for both the player and the organization. That said, New Orleans will turn to veterans Davon Godchaux, Nathan Shepherd and John Ridgeway, as well as 2025 third-round pick Vernon Broughton, who played just one game last season before suffering a season-ending injury.

But a guy I’ll have my eye on is rookie second-round pick Christen Miller, who really stood out during the preseason. His physicality could be a difference-maker for this group.

In terms of my confidence in the unit as a whole, it’s certainly not as high as some of the other groups across the roster. But the Saints invested a third- and second-round pick in interior defensive linemen in back-to-back drafts, so they’re banking on at least one of those young guys developing into a significant contributor.

4. For the first time in what seems like a long time, the Saints seem to have a viable plan at quarterback with Tyler Shough. What’s the next step in Shough’s development, how quickly do you think he can get there, and what are your expectations for him in this matchup against the Lions?

The next step for Shough is to prove that this isn’t just a fluke and that he can continue this trajectory on a consistent basis. We’ve seen the arm talent, athleticism and ability to make big-time throws in big-time moments. We’ve also seen how his teammates have gravitated toward his leadership and initiative, as well as his workout retreats with his receivers and overall time spent around the facility. Now it’s about putting all of that together for four quarters and continuing to improve while producing at a high level.

I think he can get there pretty quickly. He’s already shown that he can handle adversity and build momentum, so I’m expecting him to look confident in Detroit on Sunday. Facing a guy like Aidan Hutchinson in the season opener will be a tough task, but I’d like to see Shough play with the confidence he’s always shown, take what’s there, avoid turnover-worthy throws and make a big play or two when the opportunities come. If he can do that, I think he can get the season off to a really strong start.

5. FanDuel Sportsbook has the Lions as 6.5-point favorites over the Saints for this Week 1 matchup in Detroit. Does that spread feel too large, too little, or just about right? What do you think about the Saints’ chances at pulling off an upset?

I’d say I feel like the line is a bit large, but I would agree that the Lions should be the favorites to win this game.

That said, I wouldn’t rule out the Saints pulling off that upset. This team is hungry and ready to prove that they mean business.

Personally, I’m going to predict Detroit comes away with this one, but I expect New Orleans to put up a fight.

item.title: It took one series for Anthony Richardson to see his future with the Colts
item.description: A renewed opportunity with the Colts flashed before Richardson’s eyes.
item.content:encoded:
The first game of the NFL season is special. The NFL diluted it by moving the 22-year standard Thursday opener to Wednesday to fit a Netflix only special in on Thursday to squeeze more money out of its fans, but that’s a story for another time. Regardless, the home opener for the defending Super Bowl champs is always electric. With all that energy bouncing around, it didn’t take long for a quiet hush to fall over the festivities. With it, Anthony Richardson saw his future with the Colts. 

Sam Darnold was the bottom of the barrel until he became the top of the heap. He was a quarterback that the Jets couldn’t wait to unload after a disastrous tenure as the franchise quarterback. Yes, it took him leaving to find his footing, but a resurgence in Minnesota, followed by the greatest achievement in the game with Seattle, found him as the toast of the town and the entire league. On the first drive of the game, Darnold injured his hip and didn’t return to the field. Drew Lock stepped in and led the Seahawks to victory. 

That is the perfect example of how things can change in the NFL. The MRI for Darnold looks good, but it could have been bad, really bad. While Richardson isn’t rooting for Daniel Jones to get injured, it isn’t out of the realm of possibility that Jones misses time this season. It simply seems to be his M.O. If that happens, Richardson will be thrust into the spotlight with a chance to turn his career around. Darnold lasted one series, so that chance could present itself at any time. That should be enough of a glimpse into his Colts’ future to provide the motivation to be ready at a moment’s notice. 

Ideally, for the Colts, Anthony Richardson won’t see much time this season. That means Daniel Jones stays healthy and upright. That isn’t guaranteed, however. Sam Darnold lasted five plays. No one saw that coming. Whether one sees it coming or not, Richardson should be ready for that very scenario. Wednesday was the best glimpse he could have into his future with the Colts.

item.title: Harrison Smith: I kind of knew I'd be back the whole time
item.description: Vikings fans saluted Harrison Smith's entire career when he walked off the field at the end of Week 18 last season, but thoughts that it was the final time the safety would be on the field were premature.
item.content:encoded:
Vikings fans saluted Harrison Smith's entire career when he walked off the field at the end of Week 18 last season, but thoughts that it was the final time the safety would be on the field were premature.

Smith was out of contract throughout the offseason and preseason, but remained in touch with head coach Kevin O'Connell and agreed to return for a 15th season a few days ago. While that came as a pleasant surprise to many in Minnesota, it was something that Smith had in mind for quite a while.

"I think I kind of knew it the whole time. I just didn't know, exactly, the timing," Smith said, via the team's website.

Neither Smith nor O'Connell is ready to say that the safety will play against the Packers in Week 1. Smith has worked out with a return in mind, but acknowledged the big difference between that training and what he'll be called to do on the field.

"I'm in good shape. I've been working out," Smith said. "But there's nothing like playing football. It's just the reality of it. Heart rate, outside factors, thinking a lot while you're moving. It's hard to simulate that. I kind of do it the best I can. There's something about being on the grass and thinking while you're moving. You can feel a little stuck sometimes and just getting the fluidity back. That's kind of what I've been able to do the last few years — be very fluid out there while I'm thinking."

Smith wasn't on the injury report for Wednesday, but further word on his status for Sunday will likely come closer to kickoff.

item.title: 2026 NFL season preview, betting, odds: 1 bet I like for every AFC team
item.description: Matt Russell gives a wager he likes for all 16 AFC teams heading into the upcoming season.
item.content:encoded:
Making 32 bets before the season might feel like a lot, but when you look at how many markets are available to wager on — team futures, win totals, award markets, player props, "Game of the Year" betting, etc., it's really not all that excessive. Of course, if you had just blindly bet one unit on each of all 32 of our plays from last year's article, you'd have been up 7.26 units, and you're probably thrilled to see we're back with this article again.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL season

We'll start in the AFC, with one bet for each team in the NFL this season. 

Baltimore Ravens

The best-case scenario for Baltimore is that Jesse Minter and a bolstered defensive front works well enough that the majority of Ravens games are in control in the fourth quarter — and when they are, Derrick Henry can salt them away without Lamar Jackson needing to scramble around. 

Optimism is high for Jackson's statistics because he comes into the season healthy, but like last year, he may not stay that way. Whether that means missed time, or similar inefficiency to 2025 when he had just 349 rushing yards on 67 carries in 13 games, we'll bet Jackson — turning 30 this season — doesn't get loose frequently enough to clear this rushing total. 

Bet: Lamar Jackson under 599.5 rushing yards (-110, DraftKings)

Buffalo Bills 

Young Josh Allen didn't score nearly as many touchdowns as Allen has in his late-20s. The rushing yardage has come down over the last three seasons, but Allen has 15, 12 and 14 rushing touchdowns in those campaigns respectively, despite having James Cook available to hand the ball off to near the goal line. Until Allen wins a Super Bowl, or is dragged off the field to break his Ironman streak, he'll do anything to win games, and that means continuing to call his own number near the goal line. 

Bet: Josh Allen over 10.5 rushing touchdowns (-128, FanDuel)

Cincinnati Bengals

Long-time teammates going back to their days at LSU, Joe Burrow and Ja'Marr Chase have both been healthy for two total seasons in their professional careers. 

Chase had a 1,455-yard rookie season with eight touchdowns in 2021, and 1,700-plus yards and 17 touchdowns in 2024. The latter would have been good enough for an Offensive Player of the Year award, but Saquon Barkley went bananas that season. 

Bet: Ja'Marr Chase to win Offensive Player of the Year (10-1, FanDuel)

Cleveland Browns 

Starting with the appointment of Deshaun Watson as the No. 1 quarterback, the Browns' depth chart is full of head-scratchers. 

Upgrade to Fantasy Plus and gain your edge in player projections and much more

They could have their usual bad offense/good defense, or with new pieces and an offensive-minded head coach, the opposite, with Myles Garrett. 

The most likely result is that, intentionally or otherwise, with Watson in and Garrett off to L.A., the start of the rebuild is finally underway in Cleveland. 

Bet: Browns under 5.5 wins (+105, DraftKings)

Denver Broncos

Did Sean Payton get the final piece to unlock Denver's offense in trading for Jaylen Waddle? 

The Broncos' crowded wide receiver room had many of the same big-target players, but Waddle isn't just capable of catching a lot of balls (104 in his 2021 rookie season) or as a yards-per-catch maven (18.1 in 2022), but in a good offense with reliable quarterback play, the speedster can be a game-breaker. Luckily, because Waddle had to deal with shoddy quarterback play and was often overshadowed by running mate Tyreek Hill, he's lined below 1,000 receiving yards.

If Waddle is beset by injuries, he won't get to that number anyway, but if he's healthy, the ceiling is much higher, so it's worth taking a shot at bigger odds for a 1,250-yard season.

Bet: Jaylen Waddle: 1,250-plus receiving yards (+450, DraftKings)

Houston Texans

An under-the-radar play on the idea that Houston has a great season is DeMeco Ryans to be voted Coach of the Year. 

Expectations are high for the Texans, but they didn't win the AFC South last season, which means there is room for improvement — a necessity in voters' eyes. 

The other path to award-level credit is a gaudy record, and Houston's schedule sets up as challenging, but manageable, with the toughest games coming at home, starting with the Bills in Week 1. 

Lastly, few head coaches are associated with a dominant unit in the way that Ryans is with the Texans' top-ranked defense last season.

Bet: DeMeco Ryans to win Coach of the Year (40-1, DraftKings)

Indianapolis Colts

Before the Colts' Week 11 bye, rookie tight end Tyler Warren had nine games with a yards-per-catch rate of better than 10.0, and 61.7 receiving yards per game. 

After the bye, which included four games with either Philip Rivers or Riley Leonard at quarterback, he had none. 

With a full offseason to get ready for the rigors of 17 games, Daniel Jones back, Shane Steichen knowing what Warren's capable in the Colts' offense and the 111 targets that went to Michael Pittman in 2025 needing to go elsewhere, Warren should make a run at 100 receptions, and 1,000 yards. 

Bet: Tyler Warren: 1,000-plus receiving yards (+330, FanDuel)

Jacksonville Jaguars

Even when the future for Trevor Lawrence seemed a little dark, he was still throwing for 4,000 yards in 2022 and 2023. After playing only 10 games in 2024, Lawrence was right back to 4,000 last year, in his first season working with Liam Coen.

Coming off a division-winning season, the Jaguars' schedule is going to get tougher, and a nine-game winning streak probably isn't in the cards. However, that's a good thing for Lawrence's passing volume, as more competitive games means he'll need to throw it more often. Plus, the Jacksonville pass offense didn't even really start to click until the latter half of 2025, when Coen figured out the receiver setup for Lawrence. 

Bet: Trevor Lawrence over 3,750.5 passing yards (-114, FanDuel)

Kansas City Chiefs

With Patrick Mahomes looking set to return ready for Week 1, I assumed an under would be in order due to market overreaction. However, the expectations are relatively tempered for someone who won a Super Bowl while nursing a high-ankle sprain. 

If he's structurally functioning, Mahomes will play, and he's never thrown for fewer than 26 touchdowns in a season that he's started at least 16 games.  

The acquisition of Kenneth Walker might cut into the percentage of Chiefs' touchdowns that come through the air, but if Walker and a rebuilt O-line provide a better rushing attack between the 20s, it would give the Chiefs more opportunities near the goal line, and the volume should go up across the board. 

Mahomes still has Travis Kelce as a red zone threat, quick tosses to Xavier Worthy on the outside and Rashee Rice was only available to the Chiefs' QB for eight games last season, with five touchdown connections. Many as part of the designed tap-pass variety. 

Bet: Patrick Mahomes over 24.5 passing TDs (-130, Bet365)

Las Vegas Raiders 

In the NFL, getting a high draft pick is only relevant if you haven't already tabbed your quarterback of the future, and the last thing that Klint Kubiak (and his boss, Tom Brady) want to do is lose a lot in Vegas, during his first season as a head coach. As a result, we might see more of Kirk Cousins, and less of No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza than we might expect this season. 

Kubiak was in Minnesota from 2019 to 2021 for the best years of Cousins' career, so it's not a coincidence the two have reconnected here. If they can get on the same page, there are a few winnable games on the schedule before a late bye in Week 13. 

At 4-8 through 12 games, with an extra week to prepare, Week 14 might be the spot to give Mendoza the reins. At which point, he would have only five games to get over his prescribed passing total. 

Bet: Fernando Mendoza under 2,199.5 passing yards (-130, Bet365)

Los Angeles Chargers

Greg Roman got to drive a Ferrari when one Harbaugh gave him the Ravens' offensive coordinator job at the start of Lamar Jackson's career, but he didn't know how to drive a Lamborghini in Justin Herbert, when another tabbed him to be his OC.

Herbert started his career by averaging 287 passing yards in his first three seasons; in the last two, he's averaged 230. Part of that is due to an offensive line that lost both high-investment tackles last season, but Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater are back, and Mike McDaniel is now at the helm of an offense with the most dynamic receivers, at the right stage of their career, that Herbert has ever had. 

Situationally speaking, if former defensive coordinator Jesse Minter's departure means the Chargers are in more shootouts, that's an even better setup for McDaniel to take his high-octane QB for a spin. 

Bet: Justin Herbert over 3,599.5 passing yards (-110, Bet365)

Miami Dolphins

Maybe it's a cop-out, but we'll use a play from our look at the NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year candidates, because there's already been a development since last week's post. 

We postulated the idea that Jacob Rodriguez could have a path to starting at middle linebacker — the role of tackling-machine — over Tyrel Dodson. Sure enough, Dodson was flat-out released during cut-down day last weekend. 

Bet: Jacob Rodriguez to win Defensive Rookie of the Year (15-1, DraftKings)

New England Patriots

Teams keep trying Christian Gonzalez, because the other New England corners — Carlton Davis, Marcus Jones — are no fun to throw against either. Just 24 years old, Gonzalez is widely respected as one of the best young defensive backs in the league, but he didn't have an interception last season. He did have 10 passes defended in 14 games, so he's getting his hands on the ball, and the opportunity for bigger splash plays might come with it. 

If the Patriots' defense takes another step forward, without a clear-cut star in the front, Gonzalez could follow Patrick Surtain from 2024, when also 24 years old, he had four interceptions and won Defensive Player of the Year representing an ensemble in Denver. 

Bet: Christian Gonzalez to win Defensive Player of the Year (55-1, FanDuel)

New York Jets

Garrett Wilson is lined at 999.5 receiving yards in the prop market. 

That doesn't mean he's guaranteed to have a 1,000-yard season, but it infers that it's about 50/50. 

If Wilson does rack up 1000+ yards, it probably means Geno Smith has played pretty well for the Jets, opening the door for a big season from Wilson, on a team likely to be frequently playing from behind. 

While Wilson's injury wasn't the most serious, neither was Joe Burrow's before 2024 or Christian McCaffrey's before 2025. A good season from Smith would be something of a comeback, but he isn't returning from an injury. Meanwhile, the other pass-catchers conceptually eligible for Comeback Player of the Year have more complicated paths to a massive statistical season, and even shorter odds.

Instead of betting Wilson to get to 1,000 yards at -110 odds, let's see if Wilson can get closer to 1,300 yards and get in the mix for an award at 55-1.

Bet: Garrett Wilson to win Comeback Player of the Year (55-1)

Pittsburgh Steelers

At 40 years old, in Year 2 with the Jets, Aaron Rodgers handed the ball off to Breece Hall (209) and Braelon Allen (98) a whopping 311 times. Last year, Jaylen Warren (211) and Kenneth Gainwell (114) combined for 325 carries.

Rico Dowdle's familiar with a backfield timeshare, but he's managed near identical seasons with two teams in two seasons:

  • 2024 with Ezekiel Elliott in Dallas: 235 carries for 1,079 rushing yards

  • 2025 with Chuba Hubbard in Carolina: 236 carries for 1,076 rushing yards

Dowdle played through injury in the latter half of last season, finding a way to still get a heavy workload. Just splitting carries with Warren would mean 160, and, at his usual 4.6 yards per tote, that would add up to 736 rushing yards. All without factoring Dowdle's ability to find his way to more opportunities and production than that. 

Bet: Rico Dowdle over 699.5 rushing yards (-110, DraftKings)

Tennessee Titans

This isn't going to sound very nice. 

Cam Ward's underlying metrics were so bad last season that the Titans reached for Carnell Tate with the No. 4 pick in April's draft. However, Tate now has to line up against NFL defensive backs instead of the frequently-soft opponents on Ohio State's schedule. 

Last season, Tate had just 12 total receptions in games against Texas, Washington, Indiana and Miami, and in 2024, he had 11 total catches in games against Oregon (twice), Penn State, Indiana, Tennessee and Notre Dame.

He also has to break the huddle without Jeremiah Smith lining up on the other side of the field, getting all of a college defense's attention. Going from taking on No. 2 college corners to potentially getting the NFL's No. 1's (depending on the threat level of Calvin Ridley) is going to be a stark contrast. 

Bet: Carnell Tate under 775.5 receiving yards (-114, FanDuel)

You can find more valuable betting analysis on player props, stat leaders, and award markets from Yahoo! Sports betting contributor, Matt Russell, at THE WINDOW.

item.title: NFL survivor contest picks, predictions, advice, strategy: My favorite Week 1 selections
item.description: NFL survivor pools are back and Matt Russell runs through Week 1, giving his favorite picks to help you advance.
item.content:encoded:
You've got a better chance of stepping up into the hole against Derrick Henry than you do of stopping the momentum of NFL Survivor contests in the current football betting landscape. 

The world's largest (legal) contest, hosted at Circa Sports in Las Vegas, has over 20,000 entries for its guaranteed $20 million pool, and it's not even the biggest prize available in the space for this coming season.

The siren's song of "just" needing to pick one winner per week in America's most dissected sport makes everyone believe they can navigate the perils and potholes that the unpredictability of football supplies, but there's more to it than just "pick and pray."

Upgrade to Fantasy Plus and gain your edge in player projections and much more

Of course, you don't need to play in a high-roller edition of survivor. You, your friends, and family can play along as well here at Yahoo Sports, but a smaller pool of participants also changes the calculus when it comes to strategy. After all, the fewer the entrants, the less conceptual risk is necessary. 

Each week (until we've exhausted all reasonable paths of survival), we'll look at the Survivor Contest landscape and the best options available while understanding that it matters who you've already taken and what you might be giving up by burning a team that week. 

Week 1 moneylines

How likely is a team to win and you'll advance? The betting market provides the answer to that each week with the moneyline, which we can convert to an implied win probability.

Market power ratings

It's not as simple as picking the team most likely to win, because once you use that team, you can't use them again. What is simple is that if you're going to make it through the 18-week season, then you need to use 18 teams. That means, at some point, you'll be trusting the 18th-best team in the NFL — an unnerving thought. 

Here's a list of the current top 18 teams (with help from the betting market), and an estimation of their value to the point spread: 

  • Rams: 19.7

  • Seahawks: 18.1

  • Bills: 17.8

  • Ravens: 17.3

  • Lions: 16.7

  • Chargers: 16.7

  • Chiefs: 16.5

  • Packers: 16.5

  • 49ers: 16.5

  • Texans: 16.5

  • Eagles: 16.2

  • Patriots: 16.2

  • Bears: 15.9

  • Cowboys: 15.7

  • Broncos: 15.7

  • Bengals: 15.7

  • Jaguars: 14.6

  • Vikings: 14.0

Picking the most likely team to win each week, or the highest available team on this list above, means that you're giving up the opportunity to use them again later, and while every week is technically created equal, trusting a team in September is nerve-wracking, but doing so at some point in December is real tension. 

Week 1's top choices

As we look at the best options for Week 1 and onward, we'll be factoring in the decision tree that will sprout from that pick. The implied probability derived from the moneyline should answer any questions about why the favorite should win, but the nuance is found in what you're giving up by using them now and not later (with a projected point spread projection for those matchups). 

Jaguars (78.6%) over Browns 

Jacksonville's not the biggest favorite in Week 1, but you're backing a team that won nine straight games to end the regular season a year ago. 

On the other side, the Browns have tabbed Deshaun Watson as their starting quarterback, but there's nothing we've seen from him in Cleveland — either before he tore his Achilles in 2024 or during this preseason — that would make us think that Cleveland's offense is going to come alive. Plus, with defensive metrics that went from great to terrible depending on whether Myles Garrett was on the field, with the 2025 Defensive Player of the Year in Los Angeles, there's less to worry about for Trevor Lawrence. 

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 10 at Titans (JAX -4.5)

  • Week 12 vs. Titans (JAX -7.5)

It can be a fool's errand to try to project who the easiest matchups will be down the road, when we haven't seen anyone play in the regular season, but the Jaguars do have a pair of games with the Titans — a team that's seen money come against them in Week 1 at home … against the New York Jets. 

Chargers (80.9%) over Cardinals 

For the second spot on this list — generally reserved for a significant favorite — the game with the biggest line (and likely to be the most popular pick) does come with some trepidation. 

Cardinals QB Jacoby Brissett looked more capable last season than, say, Watson has. With legitimate weapons like Trey McBride, Marvin Harrison Jr., the emergent Michael Wilson and a pair of new running backs, combined with some uncertainty around the Chargers breaking in a new defensive coordinator — and a new offensive coordinator — and you could envision more of a sweat than you thought you were bargaining for. 

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 2 vs. Raiders (LAC -8.5)

  • Week 11 vs. Jets (LAC -8)

  • Week 16 at Dolphins (LAC -7.5)

The other reason(s) not to just roll with the chalk are that there are three other spots where the Chargers look appealing, and one is literally next week. 

At the moment, based on lookahead lines, there are two games with bigger betting lines in Week 2, and two nice options for later in the season might be enough for you to save the Chargers. 

Steelers (62.5%) over Falcons 

That the Steelers aren't even considered our "dark horse" pick only tells you how weird things might get for those either brave enough, or who are in a super-deep pool — where it's a necessity to zig while others zag. 

From a matchup perspective, if you're ever going to back a 42-year-old quarterback, doing so when the weather is warm is the time to do it. 

Aaron Rodgers' availability isn't the only consideration on the Pittsburgh side of things. For how long the defending AFC North champions will have a fully healthy defense is anyone's guess. Specifically, T.J. Watt, with whom the Steelers have a considerably better record than without, but also 37-year-old Cameron Hayward and a secondary featuring 31-year-old Jalen Ramsey and 29-year-old Jamel Dean (both older by defensive back standards). 

On the Falcons' side, Tua Tagovailoa will start Week 1, having done very little in the lead-up to the season to take the starting job from Michael Penix Jr., even as Penix Jr. recovers from ACL surgery. 

Rodgers is vulnerable against a formidable pass rush, but the Falcons are without both of 2025's highly-drafted edge rushers: Jalon Walker (season-ending injury) and James Pearce (eight-game suspension). 

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 8 vs. Browns (PIT -3)

  • Week 17 at Titans (PIT -1.5)

Before you think we're irrationally high on the Steelers this season, the fact that the other two weeks where we might consider them come with spread projections shorter than this game with the Falcons should confirm that it might be now or never for Pittsburgh. 

You'll note that the Steelers didn't make our top-18 list above, but:

  1. Pittsburgh just missed the cut, as they're bunched with the Buccaneers and Commanders around the top 20

  2. So, if you're in a contest that requires more than 18 teams selected to get to the end (like, Circa's), then the Steelers become more viable 

  3. Once you get to the top 16-24 teams in power-ranking, the order becomes personal preference

The dark horse: Raiders (61.9%) over Dolphins

There's no darker horse than the Raiders, but if you're looking for a pick with a low selection percentage, you could do worse than backing a team actively trying to win this season versus one that's more "wait-and-see."

Kirk Cousins, healthy and with his old offensive coach from when they were both with the Vikings, provides more certainty on the offensive side than the Dolphins have with new quarterback Malik Willis, who doesn't have the same roster support around him that he had in Green Bay. 

While both teams have new regimes, the Raiders are further along in their rebuilding plan. For at least one game, Las Vegas has the ideal combination of already having its potential quarterback of the future, without dealing with the growing pains of starting Fernando Mendoza just yet.

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 16 vs. Titans (LV -1)

I think you already knew there wasn't going to be another glaring spot to take the Raiders, but at least they might be favored at home against the Titans in Week 16? 

That's not something you'd want to plan for, though, as the Raiders aren't in anyone's top-18, 20, or even 25 teams, by power rating, and will likely have turned the team over to Mendoza by then.

So, maybe, if there's 20,000 other entries in your pool, finding yourself in a virtual "Black Hole," might be the way to play Week 1.

item.title: Oddsmakers react to the differing travel strategies for NFL game in Australia: 'My first thought is the Rams are nuts'
item.description: Is the Rams or 49ers' travel strategy better for a game in Australia? We asked handicappers and oddsmakers.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL will play its first-ever regular-season game in Australia later this week when the Los Angeles Rams "host" the San Francisco 49ers as 3.5-point favorites. The game will kick off at 8:35 p.m. ET on Thursday night here in the United States, but will be played at 10:35 a.m. local time on Friday morning in Melbourne. Both teams will take at least a 16-hour flight to get there — although Aaron Donald won't have to make the trip, as he was ruled out for the game on Tuesday.

To further add intrigue to the game, the teams consulted with their staffers and arrived at diametrically opposed travel strategies. The 49ers flew out on Sept. 2, and will be in Australia for about a week prior to the game, while the Rams plan to fly into Melbourne the day before the game and fly out immediately afterwards.

While the Rams are the clear Super Bowl favorite, no preseason favorite with +500 or better odds has ever won the Super Bowl over the past 30 seasons (0-for-20). And no preseason Super Bowl favorite has ever had to start its season this many time zones away on another continent — against a division opponent that could have an impact on the NFC West and No. 1 seed.

Variance provides opportunity in sports betting, and it would stand to reason that one of these strategies will be far more effective than the other. But so far, the line has held steady at Los Angeles -3.5 at sportsbooks, and the total has stuck at 48.5.

So, what is the potential betting impact of these travel strategies — both on this game and Week 2 for both teams?

We asked a bunch of oddsmakers — including one based in Australia — and handicappers for their thoughts.

It's always best to ask those with first-hand experience, so I reached out to Adam Hamilton, the head of racing and talent at Entain in Australia and New Zealand, for an on-the-ground report. While Hamilton noted the buzz surrounding the game in Melbourne and more money wagered on the Rams to cover, he was one of several oddsmakers in favor of the Rams' strategy.

"Fascinating difference in travel approach," Hamilton wrote in an email to Yahoo Sports. "Is the chance to acclimatize and settle [in] negated by the distractions and almost relaxing too much? While it's great for promotion of the game to have San Francisco here so early, I'd argue the Rams' approach is better. I love my horse racing and it's interesting most trainers would rather travel to a race interstate or overseas as close as possible."

Bet Los Angeles Rams -3.5 at sportsbooks right now

Multiple oddsmakers that Yahoo Sports spoke with noted that the travel wouldn't have an impact on the spread or the way the public bet on it. One oddsmaker said he would've opened the game Rams -4.5 if it was being played at their true home in SoFi Stadium.

"I have been pretty in the weeds on circadian rhythms for a long time," Rob Pizzola, a sharp NFL handicapper and owner of The Hammer, told Yahoo Sports via text message. "I believe the Rams' plan is better because they are going to be playing on an optimal body clock. The 49ers will get acclimated to the facility and everything else a bit better, but they are going to end up on a morning body clock in Melbourne."

Several other oddsmakers theorized that San Francisco's approach was better, in terms of being able to adjust to the time, knowing their surroundings, ability to treat injuries on the ground, etc.

Perhaps one longtime Vegas oddsmaker put it best: "My first thought is the Rams are nuts. But they had a similar strategy with a game in London and they played great. Short answer is I have no idea. Either way, I'm letting the action dictate the number."

An interesting point was raised by Dr. Cathy Anne Goldstein on Ed Feng's Power Rank podcast, though. She noted that it takes about a day per time zone crossed to fully adjust, which means that even though the 49ers were coming in a week early, they wouldn't be able to fully adjust to the time in Melbourne — needing over two weeks to do so.

"[The 49ers] are going to be partially misaligned and it's not just that internal circadian misalignment with the time in Melbourne," Dr. Goldstein said. "They're also going to have sleep deprivation and poor performance while they're training and trying to recover and optimize for themselves for the game. So I think this is not a good strategy."

With the game at 10:35 a.m. local time — which translates to 5:35 p.m. the previous day in Los Angeles or San Francisco — being partially misaligned could be an even bigger disadvantage than flying in, playing and flying out. Yahoo Sports' own Jeff Eisenberg did a deeper dive on the science behind it all in this article earlier this week.

"What the Rams are doing — their body clock is going to remained aligned to L.A. time, leading up to the game they'll be sleeping normally and training normally," Dr. Goldstein added. "I personally think this is a much better strategy to address this massive change in time zones."

Thomas Gable, sportsbook director at The Borgata in Atlantic City, added, "I asked some Australian oddsmakers and they all believe the Rams are making a big mistake in [their travel plan]. I would tend to favor the under in this game, and they're of that belief as well."

What is the impact for both teams in Week 2?

Assuming the game doesn't end in a tie, the differing travel strategies will also have an impact on the rest of the season — especially in Week 2. The 49ers return to play three straight home games (-12.5 vs. Miami Dolphins, -10.5 vs. Arizona Cardinals, -2.5 vs. Denver Broncos) and won't have to leave the West Coast again until a Week 7 game at Atlanta.

The Rams host the New York Giants in Week 2 as 9.5-point favorites, followed by consecutive road trips to Denver and Philadelphia and a home game against the Buffalo Bills. Los Angeles' schedule is far less forgiving, but the Rams may have an advantage in Week 2 by never adjusting to the Melbourne time zone.

"Maybe they're thinking ahead to Week 2, if we're not changing the body clocks then it's less of an effect," Gable added. "I believe there's going to be more of an effort to fade both of these teams in Week 2 than necessarily what happens in this week."

Either way, one team is going to end up 0-1 with a long trip back to the West Coast, and the other will likely be touting its travel plans as a big reason for a Week 1 victory.

item.title: Football fashion: 9 NFL stylists to keep an eye on during 2026 season
item.description: London Wilmot, Dex Robinson and Chad Johnson are among the NFL stylists who will be making an impact in the 2026 season with their fashion sense.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL season is off to a hot start as the Seattle Seahawks shut down the New England Patriots in a rematch of the Super Bowl on Wednesday, Sept. 9 at Lumen Field.

Besides a dominant defense that got three sacks and three interceptions, the Seahawks also looked sharp in the tunnel with a variety of subdued outfits from Jaxon Smith-Njigba and DeMarcus Lawrence. The Patriots don't have fashion-forward Stefon Diggs anymore, but fans can keep an eye on Christian Gonzalez's sleek style, especially after his big payday.

Many players don't develop their fashion sense on their own. While having a stylist used to be frowned upon because of the thought that it meant someone couldn't dress themselves, it is now practically essential. A stylist's job is to help a client's personality shine, elevate their confidence and simply take the task of finding an outfit off the to-do list.

Some of the top stylists and designers in the NFL have been piecing together outfits since long before the tunnel walk was a thing. A few have found their stride more recently as the crossover of football and fashion has expanded exponentially. What unites them is their creativity, attention to detail and heart for storytelling.

This is also a plea for the Denver Broncos to post their game day fits. They're one of the most fashionable teams in the league, but nobody knows...

Here are 9 stylists to keep an eye on this NFL season:

Infamis Missy

Infamis Missy is a Chicago-based stylist who calls herself a lifestyle architect because her work is not just about clothes, but about experiences. She is an expert in textures and colors and had one of the best looks of the entire season last year. In Week 11, she put Jaquan Brisker in a monochromatic plum 'fit that was incredible. Even though the safety now plays for the Pittsburgh Steelers, Missy will continue to work her magic to make him, and others, game day ready.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Missy - Chicago Stylist | Style & Wardrobe Pro (@infamisstyling)

Dex Robinson

You've definitely seen Dex Robinson's work, you just might not know it was done by him. He is Tyrod Taylor's right hand man and business partner in the Diallo clothing company. Besides working with the quarterback on a variety of looks, he also dressed him for his wedding! The look Taylor wore for his ceremony was a white jacket and a wide-legged pant from Louis Vuitton designed by Pharrell.

The duo is known for playing with proportions and embracing accessories to make true statements.

Chad Johnson

Not the fun-loving wide receiver. There's a new Chad Johnson making an impact in the NFL. Miami-based designer Chad Johnson has his own brand, Duane & Johnson, and he knows how to empower athletes through what they wear. He's made some standout looks for Brandon Jones, Trent Sherfield and Charles Omenihu. Johnson crafted two significant looks for Omenihu in the 2024 season: his dapper comeback look and his rockstar Super Bowl outfit.

"This season people can expect to see us push things a little further creatively, especially week 1 starting BRIGHT!" Johnson told USA TODAY Sports via text. "For me, it’s always about making sure each guy still feels like himself, just through a more elevated lens and still exploring some guys' true style that they feel their best in.

"I’ve been designing a lot more custom pieces specifically around each person, their personality and how they naturally like to dress, so nothing feels like they’re wearing a costume or nothing that’s out of place for them. Confidence is everything. There are definitely some pieces and moments coming this season that I’m really excited for people to see!"

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Chad Johnson (@mensfashionmiami)

He said that some of the ideas he and clients were working on were cut short due to injury. Jones had season-ending surgery after suffering a pectoral injury in December.

"We pulling those out for sure!" Johnson said.

London Wilmot

London Wilmot is a must-know stylist. She has been doing this for a long time and is responsible for helping build the images of CeeDee Lamb, Hollywood Brown and Tee Higgins. She has guided Pat Surtain II on his journey to become not only a shutdown defender, but one of the most fashionable players in the league.

A standout look from last season has to be for DJ Reed. Wilmot got her hands on a Prada outfit that hadn't been released to the public yet. The patchwork leather jacket is a piece of art.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by London Wilmot (@london.wilmot)

In regards to what fans can expect from her work with Surtain and Reed this season, Wilmot said, "consistency, elevated, natural outfits."

Ruggged

Evan Engram is quietly one of the most stylish players in the NFL. It's all thanks to TJ Herron, who goes by Ruggged. Week after week, the duo exemplifies luxurious coziness. The layering is always on point. There's no loud colors or extreme proportions. Everything is just classic and cool. Engram's Instagram handle is "EazyEngram" and his style surely lives up to the name.

"We’re really focused on effortlessness this year," Herron told USA TODAY via Instagram. "Last season, we really hit a stride with pairing comfort and versatility. I think this year, we’ll break that down even more with consistency and a continued veteran approach. It’s year 10 for him and I want to illustrate exactly that, continuing to push style that doesn’t have to be overtly recognizable, carrying weight through details/silhouette and really leaning into his personality.

"I’m always fine tuning things, making them 'smaller' if you will. For me it’s always less is more, and when achieved, I’ve found that generally it’s more satisfying visually and comfortable for the client physically."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Evan Engram (@eazyengram)

Haylo

Haylo is a master of separates. She puts together the coolest jacket and pants combos and knows proportions well. Last season, she worked with several Green Bay Packers players, including Dont'e Thornton Jr., Patrick Jones II and Javon Bullard. She put together a really fly look for Ernest Jones at the Super Bowl.

"I’m looking forward to continuing to grow my presence in NFL fashion this season while helping my clients build their brands and express themselves through style," she told USA TODAY via Instagram.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Haylo✨ (@styledbyhaylo)

Tom Marchitelli

Tom Marchitelli, owner of Gentleman’s Playbook, is one of the most well-known suit designers in all of sports. And rightly so. His client list is extensive and includes players from a variety of positions. He had five looks in last season's conference championships and helped Jared Verse look dapper in luxe overcoats of various colors and patterns.

But Marchitelli doesn't just do suits. He can do edgy, too. He was responsible for DeMarcus Lawrence's ultra cool Super Bowl 'fit, an all-black ensemble that featured a moto jacket and gloves.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Tom Marchitelli (@gentsplaybook)

Ini Ikpe

Ini Ikpe is another stylist who can do it all. He outfits a handful of Seattle Seahawks players and frequently collaborates with Gambia-born and Los Angeles-based designer Baba Jagne to turn heads in the tunnel. They worked together on Nick Emmanwori's incredible Super Bowl look. It was a jacket and pants set that expertly mixed black and brown leather. Even though it was the safety's rookie year, this was the statement of a sartorial sage.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Ini Sebastian Ikpe 🇳🇬 (@inisikpe)

Brian Alexander

DeVonta Smith and Brian Alexander are another dynamic duo that has elevated sports fashion. You know the monogram lapel pins? Those started as a signature of the designer's Brian Alexander Bespoke company and most likely helped revive the brooch as an "it" accessory in menswear. Alexander always nails the fit and isn't afraid to play with prints and colors. The lanky Eagles receiver isn't his only client. The designer has shown expertise for players of all sizes and shapes and wowed with Will Anderson Jr.'s NFL Honors suit. It was velvet!

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Haberdasher | 🅱️ESPOKE Suits (@brianalexanderbespoke)
